title: Đề thi thử VSTEP — Recall RV0821

passages.p1:
# Standing on Her Own Two Feet

Mai grew up in a small village where most girls were expected to marry young and depend on their husbands. From an early age, however, Mai wanted something different. She loved studying, and she dreamed of earning her own money and making her own decisions. Her parents were kind but worried; they could not understand why their daughter did not simply follow the path that everyone else took.

When Mai finished school, she made a bold choice. Instead of staying at home, she moved to the city to look for work. The first months were hard. She rented a tiny room, shared a kitchen with strangers, and often felt lonely. She took a job in a small bakery, waking before dawn to prepare bread. The pay was low, but for the first time the money she earned was truly her own.

Mai did not stop there. In the evenings, after long hours at the bakery, she attended a free class to learn accounting. She was often tired, yet she believed that new skills would open new doors. Slowly, her hard work paid off. The bakery owner noticed how careful she was with numbers and asked her to manage the shop's accounts. Her salary rose, and she began to save a little each month.

Years later, Mai opened her own small bakery. It was not large or famous, but it was hers. She chose the recipes, hired the staff and decided when to open and close. Some relatives had once whispered that a woman alone could never run a business. Mai proved them wrong, quietly and patiently, without ever raising her voice.

Today Mai often speaks to young women in her old village. She does not tell them that marriage is wrong, or that everyone must move to the city. Instead, she tells them that they should be able to choose their own lives. "Independence," she says, "does not mean doing everything alone. It means having the freedom to decide, and the confidence to try." For many of the girls who listen, her story is proof that another kind of life is possible.
passages.p2:
# Why Children Need to Move

Not long ago, most children spent much of their free time outdoors, running, climbing and playing games with friends. Today, in many countries, that picture has changed. Screens of all kinds now compete for children's attention, and busy roads and small flats leave fewer safe places to play. As a result, doctors are increasingly worried that young people are simply not moving enough.

Regular physical activity does far more than burn energy. It helps children build strong bones and muscles while their bodies are still growing, and it lowers the risk of illnesses such as obesity and heart disease later in life. Perhaps less obviously, exercise is good for the mind. Studies suggest that children who move regularly tend to sleep better, feel calmer and even concentrate more easily in class. In other words, an active child is often a happier and more focused learner.

Experts usually recommend that children get at least one hour of activity every day. This does not have to mean formal sport or expensive equipment. Everyday activities count too: walking to school, cycling, dancing in the living room, or helping in the garden. The key, specialists say, is variety and enjoyment. A child who is forced to run laps may quickly lose interest, whereas one who plays a lively game with friends barely notices the effort at all.

Parents and schools both have important roles. When adults are active themselves, children are far more likely to copy them, so a family bike ride can be more powerful than any lecture. Schools, meanwhile, can offer breaks that encourage movement rather than long periods of sitting. Some have replaced part of the timetable with short bursts of activity, and teachers report that pupils return to their desks more settled and ready to learn.

None of this means that screens are the enemy. Watching a film or playing a video game is fine in moderation, and technology can even encourage movement through dance games or fitness apps. The real problem is balance. If a child spends hour after hour sitting still, something valuable is lost. Helping young people rediscover the simple pleasure of moving their bodies may be one of the most useful gifts that adults can give them.
passages.p3:
# A Cup of Vietnam

Coffee is not native to Vietnam. It was brought by French traders in the nineteenth century, and for a long time it was grown mainly to be sent abroad. Yet over the years the Vietnamese made the drink their own, creating styles and habits found nowhere else. Today Vietnam is one of the largest coffee exporters in the world, and a cup of coffee is woven into the rhythm of daily life.

Part of what makes Vietnamese coffee special is the bean. While many countries prize the milder Arabica, Vietnam grows a great deal of Robusta, a stronger, more bitter variety that contains more caffeine. To balance this bold flavour, people traditionally add sweetened condensed milk, a habit that began when fresh milk was hard to find. The result — dark, thick coffee poured over ice and stirred with sweet milk — has become famous far beyond the country's borders.

The way the coffee is made is just as distinctive as its taste. Instead of a large machine, many Vietnamese use a small metal filter called a phin, which sits on top of the glass. Hot water drips slowly through the ground coffee, and the drinker simply waits. This unhurried process is part of the pleasure. Ordering coffee is rarely about rushing; it is an excuse to sit, watch the street and talk with friends for an hour or more.

In recent years, young people have added new ideas of their own. "Egg coffee," made with whipped egg yolk and sugar, turns a simple drink into something almost like a dessert. Chains of modern cafés now sell iced coffee in tall plastic cups to office workers in a hurry. Some older customers complain that the traditional slow style is disappearing, but others argue that coffee has always changed, and that these new versions simply continue a long story.

Whatever the style, coffee remains more than just a drink in Vietnam. It is a reason to pause, a place to meet and a small daily ritual shared by millions. For visitors, tasting a strong, sweet Vietnamese coffee is often one of the clearest ways to begin to understand the country itself.
passages.p4:
# Learning a Language by Living It

For generations, learning a foreign language meant memorising long lists of words and grammar rules, then translating sentences back and forth. Many students followed this method faithfully for years, only to find that they still froze when a real conversation began. In response, some teachers have turned to a very different idea, often called the "input" approach, which claims that we absorb a language much as children do: by understanding a great deal of it before we ever try to produce it.

According to this view, the most useful thing a learner can do is not to drill rules but to fill their days with material they can largely understand — simple stories, films with subtitles, podcasts aimed at learners. The theory holds that when the meaning is clear, the brain quietly notices patterns of grammar and vocabulary without being told them directly. Speaking and writing, supporters argue, will emerge naturally once enough has been taken in, rather like fruit that ripens only when it is ready.

The approach has obvious attractions. It is enjoyable, since learners choose content that interests them, and it removes much of the fear that comes with being forced to speak too soon. Enthusiasts point to people who have reached a high level mainly by watching television or reading novels in the target language. For such learners, the process felt less like study and more like a hobby they happened to keep up for years.

Critics, however, urge caution. They accept that plenty of input is valuable, but they doubt that it is sufficient on its own. Without some direct attention to grammar, they warn, certain errors may harden and become permanent, and progress towards accuracy can be painfully slow. Adults, unlike infants, also have limited time; few can spend the thousands of hours that a young child devotes to a first language. In practice, many teachers now favour a middle path, combining rich input with occasional explanation and plenty of speaking practice.

What almost everyone agrees on is that the old habit of studying a language purely as a set of rules, with little real contact with the language itself, rarely works well. Whether or not the input approach is followed strictly, its central lesson is hard to argue with: to learn a language, you must spend a great deal of time actually meeting it, in forms that mean something to you.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What did Mai want that was different from most girls in her village?
options: A. To support herself financially and make her own choices.
B. To marry young like the other village girls.
C. To continue her studies at a school far away.
D. To earn money mainly to support her parents.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Mai mơ tự kiếm tiền và tự quyết định, thay vì lấy chồng sớm và dựa vào chồng. B, C, D không đúng với mong muốn của cô.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What did Mai do after she finished school?
options: A. She stayed at home to help her worried parents.
B. She immediately joined a class to study accounting.
C. She went to the city in search of a job.
D. She opened a bakery straight away.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Cô lên thành phố tìm việc. A trái với lựa chọn của cô; B, D không được nhắc.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What was Mai’s first job in the city like?
options: A. It was well paid but very boring.
B. It began very early and paid little.
C. It forced her to work all through the night.
D. It was a management job from the start.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Cô làm ở tiệm bánh, dậy sớm trước bình minh, lương thấp. A, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

Why did Mai attend an accounting class in the evenings?
options: A. Because the bakery ordered her to.
B. Because the accounting class was completely free.
C. Because she hoped to feel less lonely there.
D. Because she believed new skills would help her future.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Cô tin kỹ năng mới sẽ mở ra cơ hội mới. A, B, C không phải lý do bài nêu.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

Why did the bakery owner ask Mai to manage the accounts?
options: A. He saw that she was careful and good with numbers.
B. She had just completed her accounting course.
C. The owner had no time to do the accounts himself.
D. She worked far longer hours than the others.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Chủ nhận thấy cô cẩn thận với những con số. B, C, D không được nêu.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What did Mai do years later?
options: A. She moved back to live in her old village.
B. She started and ran her own bakery.
C. She hired a manager to run the bakery for her.
D. She moved abroad to open a restaurant.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Cô mở tiệm bánh riêng và tự quản mọi thứ. A, C, D trái với bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What does "Mai proved them wrong, quietly and patiently" suggest about her?
options: A. She loudly argued with her relatives.
B. She gave up when people doubted her.
C. She asked her relatives for money.
D. She answered the doubters through steady effort, not argument.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Cô đáp lại hoài nghi bằng hành động và sự bền bỉ, không tranh cãi ồn ào. A, B, C hiểu sai thái độ của cô.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What does Mai now tell the young women in her village?
options: A. That marrying young is always a mistake.
B. That everyone must leave for the city.
C. That each of them deserves to choose her own path.
D. That they should copy her and open their own bakeries.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Cô nói họ nên được quyền tự chọn cuộc đời mình. A, B trái với lời cô; D không được nêu.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What does Mai mean when she talks about independence?
options: A. That a person must manage life entirely without others.
B. That it is about the freedom and confidence to choose.
C. That it is mainly about earning enough money to live on.
D. That women ought to refuse help from other people.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Với cô, tự lập là có tự do quyết định và tự tin để thử, chứ không phải làm mọi thứ một mình. A trái với lời cô; C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What is the main idea of the passage?
options: A. How one woman built an independent life through effort.
B. How a young woman learned to bake and sell bread.
C. How studying accounting can raise a person's salary.
D. Why everyone should leave their village for the city.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Bài kể hành trình Mai xây dựng cuộc sống tự lập, cho thấy một kiểu sống khác là có thể. B, C, D chỉ là chi tiết hoặc sai.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

How has children’s free time changed in many countries?
options: A. Children now play outdoors far more than before.
B. Children now spend most of their free time on screens.
C. Children spend less time playing actively outside.
D. Families have moved into much smaller flats.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Trẻ chơi ngoài trời ít đi vì màn hình, đường đông và chỗ ở chật. A, B, D không đúng với bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

According to the passage, physical activity helps a growing child’s body by
options: A. building stronger bones and lowering disease risk.
B. helping their bodies grow faster while they are young.
C. letting them sleep far fewer hours each night.
D. curing illnesses such as obesity and heart disease.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Vận động giúp xương-cơ chắc khỏe và giảm nguy cơ béo phì, bệnh tim. B, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What less obvious benefit of exercise does the passage mention?
options: A. It makes children need less food each day.
B. It helps children earn better exam marks in art.
C. It teaches children to use new technology.
D. It helps them sleep, stay calm and focus in class.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Vận động giúp ngủ ngon hơn, bình tĩnh hơn và tập trung tốt hơn — lợi ích cho trí óc. A, B, C không được nêu.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

How much daily activity do experts usually recommend for children?
options: A. About thirty minutes each day.
B. A minimum of sixty minutes daily.
C. Several hours of formal sport daily.
D. As little activity as possible.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Ít nhất một giờ mỗi ngày. A, C, D không đúng con số/ý bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What do specialists say is the key to keeping children active?
options: A. Making them exercise for one full hour without a break.
B. Forcing children to run laps daily.
C. Making activity varied and enjoyable.
D. Offering children prizes to reward their exercise.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Mấu chốt là sự đa dạng và niềm vui, không phải ép buộc. A, B, D trái với bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

Why does the passage say a family bike ride can be powerful?
options: A. Because cycling is the only useful exercise.
B. Because lectures almost never teach children anything.
C. Because it keeps parents away from screens.
D. Because children tend to copy active adults.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Vì trẻ dễ bắt chước người lớn năng động — làm gương mạnh hơn lời giảng. A, B, C không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What have some schools done to help pupils move more?
options: A. Added short bursts of movement to the school day.
B. Removed all breaks between lessons.
C. Made pupils sit still for longer periods.
D. Given each pupil a fitness app to follow.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Một số trường thay một phần thời khóa biểu bằng những khoảng vận động ngắn. B, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What is the passage’s view on screens?
options: A. Screens do no harm however long they are used.
B. Screens are acceptable if used in moderation.
C. Screens are the direct cause of all illness.
D. Screens should replace outdoor play entirely.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Màn hình ở mức vừa phải là ổn; vấn đề là sự cân bằng, không phải cấm hẳn. A, C, D trái với bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What does the passage suggest is the real problem?
options: A. That busy roads leave few safe places to play.
B. That schools have too many sports lessons.
C. That children no longer enjoy playing outdoors at all.
D. That too much sitting throws life out of balance.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Vấn đề là mất cân bằng — ngồi yên quá lâu. A, B, C không phản ánh ý bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What is the writer’s main message in the final paragraph?
options: A. Adults should give children more electronic gifts.
B. Helping children enjoy moving is a valuable gift.
C. Children should train hard to become athletes.
D. Parents should stop children from using phones.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Giúp trẻ tìm lại niềm vui vận động là món quà quý. A, C, D không phải thông điệp bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

How did coffee first come to Vietnam?
options: A. It grew wild in Vietnam’s forests.
B. French traders introduced it in the 1800s.
C. Chinese merchants brought it along old trading routes.
D. It arrived with the first tourists.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Do thương nhân Pháp mang tới thế kỷ 19. A, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Why is Vietnamese coffee often so strong and bitter?
options: A. Because it is always burned during roasting.
B. Because no sugar is ever added to it.
C. Because it is brewed slowly through a metal phin.
D. Because much of it is made from Robusta beans.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Vì Việt Nam trồng nhiều Robusta — mạnh, đắng, nhiều caffeine. A, B, C không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Why did people begin adding sweetened condensed milk?
options: A. Fresh milk used to be difficult to obtain.
B. It was the way French traders liked to drink it.
C. Sweeter coffee was easier to sell abroad.
D. Milk kept the iced coffee thick and cold.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Thói quen này bắt đầu khi sữa tươi khó kiếm. B, C, D không được nêu.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

What is a "phin"?
options: A. A type of sweet Vietnamese bean.
B. A large modern coffee machine.
C. A little metal dripper that sits on the cup.
D. A cloth strainer used to filter the grounds.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Phin là chiếc lọc kim loại nhỏ đặt trên miệng ly. A, B, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

What does the slow drip process suggest about drinking coffee in Vietnam?
options: A. People want their coffee as fast as possible.
B. Coffee is meant to be enjoyed slowly and socially.
C. The filter makes the coffee taste weaker.
D. Drinkers usually leave before it is ready.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Sự thong thả là một phần thú vui — cà phê là dịp để ngồi lâu, trò chuyện. A, C, D trái với bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

What is "egg coffee" described as?
options: A. A sweet, creamy drink close to a pudding.
B. An old recipe brought by French traders.
C. A quick iced drink sold to office workers.
D. A bitter coffee served without any sugar.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Nó biến thức uống đơn giản thành thứ gần như món tráng miệng. B, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Why do some older customers complain about modern cafés?
options: A. The new coffee is far too bitter for them.
B. The cafés no longer sell any iced coffee.
C. They feel the slow, traditional style is fading.
D. Young people have introduced too many new recipes.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Họ tiếc phong cách chậm rãi truyền thống đang mất đi. A, B, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

How do others respond to the worry that tradition is being lost?
options: A. They agree that all change should be stopped.
B. They say only tourists should drink coffee.
C. They believe coffee will soon disappear.
D. They see the new styles as part of an ongoing story.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Họ cho rằng cà phê vốn luôn đổi thay; phiên bản mới chỉ tiếp nối câu chuyện dài. A, B, C không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

According to the passage, coffee in Vietnam is mainly
options: A. a social ritual, not only a drink.
B. a product made only for foreign markets.
C. a modern habit among office workers.
D. a custom followed mostly by the older generation.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Cà phê là dịp dừng lại, chỗ gặp gỡ, nghi thức hằng ngày — hơn cả thức uống. B, C, D thu hẹp hoặc sai.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Why does the writer say tasting the coffee helps visitors?
options: A. It is an easy way to meet local people.
B. It proves the coffee is stronger than at home.
C. It offers a clear way into understanding the country.
D. It guarantees they will move to Vietnam.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Vì đó là cách rõ nhất để bắt đầu hiểu về đất nước. A, B, D không phản ánh ý bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What problem with the traditional method does the passage describe?
options: A. It made learners forget new words within weeks.
B. It succeeded only with learners who read novels.
C. It explained grammar rules but ignored the exceptions.
D. Learners still struggled to speak in real situations.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Dù học quy tắc và dịch nhiều năm, học viên vẫn lúng túng khi trò chuyện thật. A, B, C không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What is the central claim of the "input" approach?
options: A. Grammar rules must be memorised before anything else.
B. We learn best by understanding a lot before speaking.
C. Translation is the fastest route to fluency.
D. Speaking should always come before listening.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Ta tiếp thu ngôn ngữ như trẻ con — hiểu thật nhiều trước khi tạo ra nó. A, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

The comparison with "fruit that ripens only when it is ready" is used to suggest that
options: A. learners should choose only material that feels easy.
B. language skills decay quickly if unused.
C. output appears naturally after enough input, not before.
D. grammar must be corrected as early as possible.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Nói/viết sẽ tự đến khi đã tiếp nhận đủ — không nên ép sớm. A, B, D hiểu sai phép so sánh.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

Why do enthusiasts find the approach appealing?
options: A. It is enjoyable and reduces the fear of early speaking.
B. It promises complete fluency within just a single week.
C. It works even when the material is far too hard.
D. It focuses mainly on translating long classic novels.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Nó thú vị và gỡ bỏ nỗi sợ khi bị ép nói sớm. B, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What is the critics’ main worry about relying on input alone?
options: A. That learners will lose interest in stories.
B. That input is far too difficult to find.
C. That children learn faster than any adult.
D. That errors may stick and accuracy may improve slowly.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D. Không chú ý ngữ pháp thì lỗi có thể thành cố tật và tiến bộ về độ chính xác rất chậm. A, B, C không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

Why does the passage mention that adults have "limited time"?
options: A. To prove that children do not study grammar.
B. To show adults should give up learning languages.
C. To question whether input alone is practical for adults.
D. To stress how many hours children give their first language.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C. Để chỉ ra người lớn khó bỏ ra hàng nghìn giờ như trẻ nhỏ, nên chỉ input thôi có thể không thực tế. A, B, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What "middle path" do many teachers now favour?
options: A. Dropping input and returning to pure grammar drills.
B. Mixing lots of input with some grammar and speaking.
C. Enjoying podcasts and subtitles but skipping grammar entirely.
D. Translating every sentence word by word.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Kết hợp đầu vào phong phú với đôi lúc giải thích và nhiều luyện nói. A, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What is the writer’s attitude towards the input approach?
options: A. Broadly sympathetic but in favour of a balanced version.
B. Strongly opposed to using input of any kind.
C. Sure it is the one method guaranteed to work.
D. Mainly critical, stressing the errors that input can leave.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Người viết nhìn nhận cân bằng: công nhận giá trị cốt lõi nhưng nghiêng về cách kết hợp, không tán dương tuyệt đối. B, C, D thái quá một chiều.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What do almost all sides agree on, according to the passage?
options: A. That grammar explanations are entirely a waste of time.
B. That memorising rules without genuine exposure seldom succeeds.
C. That adults should learn exactly as young children do.
D. That subtitles should be banned for learners.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Học thuần quy tắc, ít tiếp xúc thật với ngôn ngữ, hiếm khi hiệu quả. A, C, D trái với bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What is the "central lesson" the writer draws at the end?
options: A. You need plenty of real, meaningful exposure to it in use.
B. You should memorise as many rules as possible.
C. You should rely on films instead of reading novels.
D. You should avoid speaking until you are perfect.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A. Muốn học ngôn ngữ phải dành nhiều thời gian thật sự tiếp xúc với nó, dưới hình thức có ý nghĩa với mình. B, C, D không đúng.

questions.content:
writing — Task 1

Your friend has heard that you won two tickets to a concert and has written to ask you about it. Write a letter to your friend. In your letter, you should: 1. tell your friend where and when the concert is and who will be performing 2. explain how you managed to get the two tickets 3. suggest how your friend could get tickets too

writing — Task 2

You should spend about 60 minutes on this task. These days, more and more people manage their money through online banking and pay for things by scanning QR codes with their phones. Supporters say these services are fast and convenient, while others worry about the dangers they may bring. What are the benefits and the potential risks of online banking and QR-code payments? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write an essay of at least 250 words.

speaking — Part 2

Situation: Your school has asked you to organise a festival for students, and you must decide what kind of festival it will be. You are considering the following options: 1. A music festival with live performances 2. A food festival where students cook and sell dishes 3. A handicraft festival where students make and display crafts Which one would you choose? Why?

speaking — Part 3

Topic: Choosing a new job is an important decision, and people weigh up several things before they accept an offer. Talk about the main things a person should consider when choosing a new job and which one matters most. Ideas: - The salary and benefits - The working environment - The chance to develop and be promoted - Your own idea Further questions: 1. Is a high salary more important than enjoying the work? Why? 2. How can someone find out what a company is really like before accepting a job? 3. Should young people change jobs often or stay with one employer for a long time?
